source.title: Biosynthesis of Fatty Acids & Eicosanoids
source.section: The chapter discusses the biosynthesis of fatty acids and eicosanoids, focusing on the pathways and regulation of lipogenesis in the cytosol.

chunks.text:
Fatty acids are synthesized by an extramitochondrial system. The extramitochondrial system is responsible for the complete synthesis of palmitate from acetyl-CoA in the cytosol. In most mammals, glucose is the primary substrate for lipogenesis. Critical diseases of the lipogenesis pathway have not been reported in humans. Inhibition of lipogenesis occurs in type 1 diabetes mellitus. Variations in the activity of lipogenesis affect the nature and extent of obesity.

Unsaturated fatty acids in phospholipids of the cell membrane are important in maintaining membrane fluidity. A high ratio of polyunsaturated fatty acids to saturated fatty acids in the diet is beneficial in preventing coronary heart disease. Animal tissues have limited capacity for desaturating fatty acids. Certain dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids are required, which are derived from plants. Eicosanoic fatty acids give rise to eicosanoids such as prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and lipoxins. Prostaglandins mediate inflammation. Prostaglandins mediate pain. Prostaglandins induce sleep. Prostaglandins regulate blood coagulation. Prostaglandins regulate reproduction. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen inhibit prostaglandin synthesis. Leukotrienes have muscle contractant properties. Leukotrienes have chemotactic properties. Leukotrienes are important in allergic reactions. Leukotrienes are important in inflammation.

The main pathway for de novo synthesis of fatty acids occurs in the cytosol.

The main pathway for de novo synthesis of fatty acids is present in many tissues, including liver, kidney, brain, lung, mammary gland, and adipose tissue.

Acetyl-CoA is the immediate substrate for fatty acid synthesis.

Free palmitate is the end product of fatty acid synthesis.

chunks.text: The initial step in fatty acid synthesis is the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to form malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase. The reaction requires ATP and the B vitamin biotin. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is a multienzyme protein containing biotin carboxylase, a carboxyl transferase, and a biotin carrier protein which binds biotin. The reaction takes place in two steps. Step 1 is catalyzed by biotin carboxylase, resulting in the carboxylation of biotin and uses ATP. Step 2 is catalyzed by carboxyl transferase, resulting in the transfer of the carboxyl group to acetyl-CoA, forming the product, malonyl-CoA (Figure 23-1). Acetyl-CoA carboxylase has a major role in the regulation of fatty acid synthesis. Biotin is covalently linked to the biotin carrier protein.

chunks.text: The fatty acid synthase complex is a homodimer of two identical polypeptide chains. Each chain of the fatty acid synthase complex contains six enzyme activities and the acyl carrier protein (ACP). The fatty acid synthase complex is arranged in an X shape, as shown by X-ray crystallography. The enzymes in the fatty acid synthase complex are linked in a specific sequence in the primary structure of the protein. The acyl carrier protein (ACP) contains 4'-phosphopantetheine, which includes the vitamin pantothenic acid. The structure of the fatty acid synthase complex allows for the compartmentalization of the fatty acid synthesis process within the cell without the need for permeability barriers. All enzymes in the fatty acid synthase complex are synthesized coordinately because they are encoded by a single gene.

chunks.text: Fatty acid synthesis begins with the combination of acetyl-CoA with a cysteine —SH group on the ACP of one monomer of the fatty acid synthase complex (Figure 23–3, reaction 1a). Malonyl-CoA combines with the adjacent —SH on the 4'-phosphopantetheine of the ACP of the other monomer (reaction 1b). These reactions are catalyzed by malonyl acetyl transacylase. The reaction forms 3-ketoacyl enzyme (acetoacetyl enzyme). Decarboxylation facilitates the reaction's completion by pulling the sequence of reactions forward. The 3-ketoacyl group undergoes reduction by 3-ketoacylreductase. The 3-ketoacyl group undergoes dehydration by dehydratase. The 3-ketoacyl group undergoes further reduction by enoyl reductase to form a saturated acyl enzyme. The saturated acyl residue transfers from the —SH of the 4' phosphopantetheine to the free cysteine —SH group. The transfer makes way for a new malonyl-CoA. This cycle repeats six more times until a saturated 16-carbon acyl radical (palmitoyl) is assembled. The palmitoyl is released from the enzyme complex by thioesterase. Free palmitate must be activated to acyl-CoA to proceed in other metabolic pathways. Possible fates for palmitate include esterification into acylglycerols, chain elongation, desaturation, or esterification into cholesteryl ester.

The oxidative reactions of the pentose phosphate pathway are the chief source of the hydrogen required for the synthesis of fatty acids. Tissues specializing in active lipogenesis, such as the liver, adipose tissue, and the lactating mammary gland, possess an active pentose phosphate pathway. Both the pentose phosphate pathway and lipogenesis occur in the cytosol of the cell, eliminating membranes or permeability barriers against the transfer of NADPH.

Other sources of NADPH include the reaction that converts malate to pyruvate catalyzed by the NADP malate dehydrogenase (malic enzyme) (Figure 23-4). The extramitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase reaction is another source of NADPH, particularly in ruminants.

chunks.text: Arachidonate and other C20 polyunsaturated fatty acids give rise to eicosanoids. Eicosanoids include prostaglandins (PG), thromboxanes (TX), leukotrienes (LT), and lipoxins (LX). Eicosanoids are physiologically and pharmacologically active compounds. Eicosanoids are considered to act as local hormones. Eicosanoids function through G-protein–linked receptors to elicit their biochemical effects. There are three groups of eicosanoids synthesized from C20 eicosanoic acids. C20 eicosanoic acids are derived from the essential fatty acids linoleate and α-linolenate. Eicosanoids are also derived from dietary arachidonate and eicosapentaenoate. Arachidonate is usually derived from the position 2 of phospholipids in the plasma membrane. Phospholipase A2 acts on phospholipids to release arachidonate. Arachidonate is the substrate for the synthesis of PG2 and TX2 series by the cyclooxygenase pathway. Arachidonate is also the substrate for the synthesis of LT4 and LX4 series by the lipoxygenase pathway. The cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways compete for arachidonate. The subscript in eicosanoid names denotes the total number of double bonds in the molecule and the series to which the compound belongs. (Figure 23–10)

Prostanoids are synthesized by many different cell types, but each cell type produces only one type of prostanoid. Cyclooxygenase is a 'suicide enzyme,' meaning it undergoes self-catalyzed destruction, which contributes to the 'switching off' of prostaglandin activity. Prostaglandins are rapidly inactivated by 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase. Sulfasalazine and indomethacin can block this enzyme, thereby prolonging the half-life of prostaglandins in the body.
